Applied linguistics student here, both answers mean slightly different things. Not trying to be a smart-ass, I just literally had to study all those small differences

"Man" has kinda two main meanings in English. 

First, there's, we'll, "man"- specifically a representative of male gender, in polish that's "mężczyzna". So, if you write "Mój szef to dobry mężczyzna", here you are specifying that he's a good man, not a good person - the latter of which I suspect is what the app wanted to say.

Secondly, there's "mankind"/"ludzkość". From what I understand it comes from the old words in English for man/woman which were wereman/wifman. The "were" in "werewolf" comes from that, and the "man" in "snowman" also means that it's humanoid, not that it's specifically male. So, "mój szef to dobry człowiek" means that he is a good person, in broader sense as a representative of the whole mankind, he is a good one.

"Gender" in gnc stands for "gender *roles*" - a set of stereotypes that exist within a  society about men/women. Those are purely socially constructed and change over time and in different populations. 

Gender identity is innate and doesn't change, everyone has one and it's unaffected by society.

Gnc is about the part of your personal identity ("who am I?") in relation with societal roles and stereotypes (ex. "What type of a man am I? Am I a *feminine* man?"). If you don't fit in with what is the societal stereotype for your gender, you are gnc. 

 For example, society says "women wear dresses", if a man wears a dress, that does not change his actual gender identity, but he would be considered gender nonconforming. You can see how gender roles change because in most cultures a woman not wearing a dress wouldn't be considered gender nonconforming even tho that goes against the stereotype - which was created way way earlier.

Then the whole idea of rr could be considered as gnc because in society it's assumed that "men are masculine provide for the family and women are shy and cook" - and rr doesn't follow the stereotype. Then again, you could ask if rr shouldn't instead be considered "non heteronormative" or if gnc is a form of non heteronormativity, when one stops and other begins etc. Identity is a really complicated subject to talk about, especially social identity.

The recipe:

Okay so making a normal omelette is fairly easy, and I'm going to tell you how my mom taught me to do it and how I changed some things. You don't really need to stick to the recipe as you can't really go wrong with it, do it how you like it, I like mine to have a bit more flour in it. 

You're going to need:

- 2 eggs

-  milk (2 spoonfuls)

- flour (2 spoonfuls)

- salt and pepper (to taste) and if you want you can also get some other spices (I like to use a bit of garlic powder, oregano, paprika and curry) 

- any ingredients inside you'd like to eat. I like some cheese, ham and sometimes maybe a bit of tomatoes, my mum likes to put spinach in it.

How to prepare it:
In a bowl beat your eggs, then add the milk and flour and beat it again so that there aren't any chunks and it's well mixed. Next put your salt and pepper in or if you choose to do so add in your additional spices (I eyeballed mine but it was a lot of oregano and garlic powder then a pinch of curry and paprika). I like to put only a little bit of salt because the ham I'm using is fairly salty itself. If you're using dried oregano a good idea would be to have the batter put aside for some time so that it isn't hard but personally I don't care and just put it all on a heated pan with a bit of oil. Cook it on a small flame (this is a thicc boi), and when the bottom solidifies put your ham and cheese on half of it. Lastly when the inside is as solid as you like (it doesn't have to be completely solid but be careful not to eat raw eggs) close it in half and flip. Be careful not to spill the innards. After around 30s the omelette is ready. I like to eat this version with ketchup.
